input:
Notes from a talk on on-call at a mid-size infra team.

Their pager load dropped by about 60% in two quarters, and the speaker said almost none of it came from fixing bugs. It came from deleting alerts. Every alert had to name the action a human would take when it fired; if nobody could name one, the alert was turned into a dashboard panel instead. They also moved from "page on symptoms and causes" to "page on symptoms only": high error rate or latency users can feel pages someone, a full disk on one replica opens a ticket.

The second change was a rule that whoever gets paged for an alert three times in a month owns making it go away that month, ahead of feature work. The speaker called this "making the pain land on the people who can remove it".

Third: runbooks live next to the alert definition in the same repo, and an alert without a runbook link fails CI.

My note: we page on disk usage and on single-node CPU right now. Bring this to Thursday's ops review.

Kalman filter, finally clicked: it's a weighted average of what the model predicted and what the sensor measured, and the weight is how uncertain each one is. Low sensor noise -> trust the measurement more. Then the uncertainty itself gets updated every step. Remember this for the rover odometry project.

Highlights from a chapter on feedback loops in a systems-thinking book.

A stock is anything that accumulates: water in a bathtub, money in an account, trust in a team. Flows change stocks: inflows fill, outflows drain. You cannot change a stock instantly, only its flows, which is why stocks act as buffers and why systems lag.

A balancing loop pushes a stock toward a goal (a thermostat). A reinforcing loop amplifies whatever is happening (interest compounding, a rumor spreading). Most surprising behavior comes from delays: when the information about a stock arrives late, people overshoot, like adjusting a shower that takes ten seconds to change temperature.

The author's warning: the leverage points people reach for first, like adjusting parameters (tax rates, budgets), are usually the weakest. Changing the goal of a system or who gets which information is far stronger.

From a cooking class tonight. Why my steaks come out grey: the pan was crowded and the meat was wet. Browning (Maillard reaction) only gets going above roughly 140C, and water on the surface holds the surface near 100C until it evaporates. So: pat the meat dry, salt it at least 40 minutes ahead or right before (not in between, when the salt has pulled out water that hasn't been reabsorbed), preheat the pan until a drop of water skitters, and leave space between pieces so steam escapes. Flip once a crust forms; it releases from the pan on its own.

Reading on fund fees. A fund charging 1% a year versus one charging 0.05%: on a 7% return over 30 years, $10,000 grows to about $57,000 at 6% net and about $74,000 at 6.95% net. The fee difference costs about a quarter of the final balance, and it compounds just like returns do. Most actively managed funds trail their index after fees over 15 years (the SPIVA scorecards put it above 85% for large-cap US funds). Takeaway for me: check the expense ratio on the 401k options before the rollover.
